title: The Taxonomy of Touch
hook: Touch is the channel with the fewest words and the strictest rules, and the only one where a reading can never replace asking.
why:
Touch is the oldest channel people have. Before an infant can see clearly or understand a word, it is held, fed, rocked and soothed by touch, and touch remains the most direct way one body can affect another. It can comfort a grieving friend more than any sentence, and it can frighten, humiliate or harm more than any look. No other channel carries such strong rules, and no other channel is so often misread with such serious consequences.

This chapter maps the territory. You will learn the main kinds of touch and why confusing them causes trouble, how a single touch can carry many meanings, how relationships draw maps of where on the body each person may touch, why skin is built to register care, how touch follows lines of power, and why the response to a touch tells you more than the touch itself. It ends with the rule that sets touch apart from everything else in this book: you can read a face or a posture without asking, but you can never read your way to permission to touch. Only a clear yes does that.

teach.h: Touch comes in kinds, and confusing them causes trouble.
teach.p:
In 1974 the psychologist Richard Heslin proposed a way of sorting touch into five broad kinds, arranged roughly by intimacy. Functional and professional touch is the touch of a doctor, a barber, a physiotherapist or a tailor, in which the toucher's role gives permission and the touch serves a task. Social and polite touch is the handshake, the brief tap to get attention, the guiding hand at a doorway. Friendship and warmth includes the pat on the back, the arm round the shoulder, the hug between friends. Love and intimacy is the long embrace, the held hand, the stroke of the hair. Sexual touch is its own category, with its own rules.

The categories overlap, and people disagree about where particular touches belong, but the idea behind them is useful. Many of the worst misunderstandings about touch are category errors: a social touch read as friendship, a friendly touch read as intimate, an intimate touch offered where only a polite one was welcome. A doctor's examination is acceptable because both people understand it as functional. The same touch from someone without that role would be an assault.

Categories also change with setting. A hug that is ordinary between friends in a pub may be unwelcome between the same two people in an office. A hand on the arm that is normal in one family or culture may feel intrusive in another.

So the first question about any touch is not *what does it mean?* but *what kind of touch is this, for these two people, here?* If you cannot answer that confidently, you are already in uncertain territory, and the rest of this chapter suggests how to proceed.
teach.disconfirm: If touches in your circle were almost never misread between kinds, so that a friendly touch was never taken as more and a polite one never as less, the category idea would add little for you. Most people can recall at least one category error, given or received.

teach.h: The same touch can mean many things.
teach.p:
In 1985 Stanley Jones and Elaine Yarbrough asked people to record, as soon as possible after it happened, every time someone touched them over several days: who, where on the body, in what situation, and what the touch seemed to mean. From hundreds of such records they identified a range of meanings, grouped into clusters including warmth and support, playfulness, attempts to control or direct, ritual greetings and departures, touches in the course of a task, and accidents.

The same physical touch appeared in many clusters. A hand on the shoulder could be support for someone upset, a way of getting attention, a request to move, a greeting, a playful nudge or an attempt to assert control. What decided its meaning was not the touch itself but the relationship, the situation, the timing, the pressure and duration, and what was said alongside it.

This is the theme of every chapter in this book, and it applies with special force to touch. There is no dictionary entry for a hand on the shoulder, just as there is none for folded arms. A touch is a move in a relationship, and it means what the relationship and the moment make it mean.

For a reader watching others, the lesson is to read touch in its full context before deciding what it says about two people. For someone deciding whether to touch, it is a warning: the meaning you intend is not necessarily the meaning that arrives. You may offer support and be felt as controlling, or offer warmth and be felt as intrusive.

A touch says what the relationship lets it say, and sometimes more than you meant.
teach.disconfirm: If people in your life consistently understood your touches exactly as you intended them, whatever the relationship and setting, the gap between intended and received meaning would be small for you. Asking one or two of them would tell you whether that is so.

teach.h: Relationships draw maps of permission on the body.
teach.p:
In 2015 Juulia Suvilehto, Lauri Nummenmaa, Robin Dunbar and colleagues asked over thirteen hundred people in Finland, France, Italy, Russia and the United Kingdom to colour in, on outline drawings of the body, where each of a long list of people would be allowed to touch them: a partner, a parent, a sibling, a close friend, an acquaintance, a stranger, and so on.

The maps were strikingly consistent. The closer the emotional bond, the more of the body a person was allowed to touch. Partners could touch almost anywhere. Close family and friends could touch the head, arms, shoulders and back. Acquaintances were mostly limited to the hands and arms, and strangers to the hands alone. The same basic pattern appeared in all five countries, though some cultures allowed more touch overall than others.

These maps explain why some touches feel wrong even when nothing about them is hostile. An acquaintance who touches your face or your waist has used a map that belongs to a closer relationship than the one you have. The discomfort is the feeling of a boundary crossed, the same alarm the chapter on proxemics described, but sharper.

Everyone carries their own map, shaped by family, culture, history and temperament. People who have been hurt may have much smaller maps than average. People raised in physically affectionate families may have larger ones. You cannot see another person's map, and you cannot safely assume it matches yours.

When in doubt, assume the map is smaller than yours, and let the other person widen it if they wish.
teach.disconfirm: If people's maps of where others may touch them did not depend on how close the relationship was, the research described here would be wrong. In your own life, notice whether the touches that felt intrusive came from people further away on the map than the touch implied.
teach.pullQuote: You cannot see another person's map, and you cannot safely assume it matches yours.

teach.h: Skin is built to feel care.
teach.p:
Touch is not only a social signal. The skin has nerve fibres that seem specialised for it. In 2009 Line Löken, Håkan Olausson and colleagues recorded the activity of single nerve fibres in people's arms while stroking the skin at different speeds. A class of slow-conducting fibres, known as C-tactile afferents, responded best to gentle stroking at about the speed of a caress, and the more strongly they fired, the more pleasant people rated the touch. Faster and slower strokes produced less activity and less pleasure.

Touch can also carry specific feelings. In 2006 Matthew Hertenstein, Dacher Keltner and colleagues asked strangers to communicate emotions to each other by touching only the other person's forearm, with a barrier between them so that nothing could be seen. Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy at rates well above chance, from touch alone.

And touch can lighten a load. The chapter on the quiet body in Part VI described a study in which holding a partner's hand reduced the brain's response to the threat of a shock, most of all in the happiest marriages.

All of this explains why touch is so powerful and so risky. The same channel that can soothe with remarkable directness can also intrude with remarkable directness. The nerves that register a welcome caress register an unwelcome one just as clearly, and the feeling that follows is the opposite of comfort.

Touch reaches people more directly than anything else you can do, which is exactly why it requires their agreement.
teach.disconfirm: If gentle touch from a trusted person felt no more pleasant or calming than any other touch, the findings on caress-tuned nerves and stress would not apply to you. Such individual differences exist, which is another reason to ask rather than assume.

teach.p:
In the 1970s the psychologist Nancy Henley observed that touch often flows down hierarchies. Bosses touch employees on the shoulder more than employees touch bosses; doctors touch patients; teachers touch pupils; older people touch younger ones. She argued that the freedom to touch without asking is itself a privilege of status. Later observational research, including work by Judith Hall, found the pattern weaker and more dependent on setting than Henley had proposed, but the asymmetry she noticed is still worth watching for.

The question to ask about any touch between people of unequal power is whether it could easily be refused. A manager who puts a hand on an employee's shoulder during a review, a senior colleague who hugs a junior at a party, a coach who pats a young player: in each case the person being touched may not feel free to step away, object or say no, and their stillness tells you nothing about their wishes.

For a reader, this means watching who touches whom, and whether the touch is returned. Touch that runs only one way between two people is often telling you about the relationship's power, not its warmth. Touch that is returned in kind, at a similar level, is more likely to be mutual.

For someone with power, it means a higher bar. Where you hold authority over someone, choose words instead of touch unless they have clearly invited it, and pay attention to any sign that your touch is being endured rather than welcomed. The chapter on the ethics of reading people makes the same point about readings: the more power you hold, the higher the standard.

The freedom to touch without asking is a privilege. Use it as little as possible.
teach.disconfirm: If touch between people of unequal power in your setting turned out to be returned as often by the junior as by the senior, and refused as easily, the asymmetry would not be operating there. Watch a few such relationships before assuming either way.

teach.h: Read the response, not the touch.
teach.p:
The most informative part of any touch is how the person touched responds. Do they lean into it, relax, return it? Or do they stiffen, go still, shift their weight away, end the conversation, or glance towards someone else? Responses unfold over a second or two, and they are often clearer than anything the toucher intended.

Be especially careful with stillness. A person who does not move away from a touch has not necessarily welcomed it. People often freeze when touched unexpectedly or unwantedly, particularly by someone with power, someone larger, or someone whose reaction they fear. Freezing is a common response to threat, and the chapters of Part II discuss it further. It looks like acceptance from the outside, and it is not.

The response can also change over time. Someone who welcomed a hug a year ago may not welcome one now, after a loss, an illness, an argument or a change in the relationship. Every touch is a new question, and the last answer does not settle the next.

A short word on influence. Some studies have reported that a brief touch on the arm can increase compliance or generosity, for example tips in restaurants, in what was called the Midas touch. The findings are mixed. Either way, touching people in order to influence them is a technique of the kind this book refuses to teach. It uses the most direct channel a body has for a purpose the other person has not agreed to.

Read the response, and take anything short of a clear welcome as a reason to stop.
teach.disconfirm: If people who froze when touched turned out, when asked later, to have welcomed the touch as often as people who leaned into it, stillness would be a weaker warning sign than this block claims. The research on freezing under threat, and many people's accounts, suggest otherwise.

teach.h: Touch is the one channel where you must ask.
teach.p:
Every other chapter in this book teaches you to read without asking, and then to ask when it matters. Touch reverses the order. With touch, reading is never enough. The statement at the front of this book puts it plainly: in touch, closeness and sex, the only signal that grants permission is a clear yes, and no posture overrides a word.

Asking can be simple and light. *Hug?* with open arms that can easily turn into a handshake. *Is it all right if I put my hand on your shoulder?* when someone is upset. A hand offered rather than a hand taken. Waiting for the other person to complete a gesture you have started. The chapter on consent in Part III treats this in depth.

Children deserve the same respect. A child who stiffens and turns away when relatives insist on a goodbye hug is telling you something about their own body, and making them comply teaches them that their body's signals do not count. Offering a wave or a high five instead teaches them the opposite.

Culture, religion and history shape what people will welcome. In some traditions, touch between men and women outside the family is not appropriate at all, and a handshake declined is a matter of faith, not rudeness; Part V discusses this. Men's touch with other men carries its own rules and its own costs, which Part III explores. People who have experienced violence may need much more space than their friends realise.

Read everything else. Ask about touch.
teach.disconfirm: If asking before touching made people consistently less comfortable than touching without asking, by their own account, the rule would cost more than it protects. Most people, asked, say they prefer being asked, and the cost of a wrong guess is far higher than the cost of a question.

poseGallery.doCaption: Matching the touch that was offered.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hugging a colleague who offered a handshake.
poseGallery.annotation: Category errors cause most trouble with touch. Meet the level the other person offers, and let them raise it if they wish.

poseGallery.doCaption: Arm back, still side by side, still close.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Keeping an arm round someone who has gone stiff.
poseGallery.annotation: The response tells you more than the touch. Stiffening, stillness and shifting weight are reasons to stop, without fuss.

poseGallery.doCaption: Words instead of touch, where power runs one way.
poseGallery.dontCaption: A hand on the shoulder of someone who cannot easily refuse it.
poseGallery.annotation: Touch often flows down hierarchies. Where you hold power, the bar for touching should be higher, not lower.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading her stillness as a yes.
poseGallery.annotation: People often freeze when touched unwantedly, and stillness is not consent. Only a clear yes grants permission.

caseStudy:
Dan, forty-two, coaches an under-twelves football team on Saturday mornings. He grew up in a family that hugged and slapped backs, and he coaches the same way: a pat on the back after a good pass, a hand on the shoulder when explaining a drill, a ruffle of the hair after a goal. Most of the boys seem to like it.

In his second season a new boy, Kai, joins the team. After Kai scores in his first match, Dan claps him on the back. Kai flinches, his shoulders jump up, and he steps sideways out from under the hand. He says nothing and runs back to his position. Dan notices it and, for once, does not do it again.

Over the next few weeks he watches more carefully, not only Kai but the whole team. He notices that two other boys also go still when patted, smiling politely but holding their arms tight to their sides. He had been reading their stillness as acceptance. He also notices that several boys initiate contact themselves: they run up for a high five, or bump his fist.

Dan changes his habit. He offers a raised hand for a high five or a fist bump and lets each boy choose whether to complete it. He explains drills with words and demonstrations instead of steering boys by the shoulders. When a boy is upset, he crouches beside him and asks what happened, rather than putting an arm round him straight away.

Kai's mother mentions at the end of the season that Kai has sensory sensitivities and that unexpected touch is genuinely painful for him. She thanks Dan for the high fives. Kai, she says, likes being able to decide. Dan realises that the boys who used to go still were telling him the same thing, and that most of them now choose the fist bump.
observe: In a public place, notice touches between people you can see, and for each ask what kind of touch it was and how the person touched responded.
Notice who touches whom in a workplace or family gathering, and whether the touches are returned at the same level.
The next time you touch someone, even briefly, watch their response for the following two seconds.

drills.name: Touch Diary
steps: For two days, write down every time someone touches you or you touch someone, as soon as you can afterwards.
For each, note who, where on the body, the situation, and what kind of touch it was.
Note what you think the touch meant, and how it felt.
Mark any touch that felt like a different kind from the one intended.
At the end, write one pattern you notice in your own touching.

drills.name: Your Own Map
steps: Draw a simple outline of a body, front and back.
For three people, a close friend, a colleague and an acquaintance, shade where each could touch you comfortably.
Compare the three maps.
Think of one person whose touch has felt intrusive, and mark where it fell on the map for your relationship.
Write down what that tells you about maps that differ from yours.

drills.name: Response Watch
steps: Over a week, watch for touches between other people in public places, in films or in your workplace.
For each, note the response of the person touched in the following two seconds.
Sort the responses into welcoming, neutral, stiffening or freezing, and moving away.
Note any case where the toucher did not seem to notice the response.
Write one sentence about what you would have done in the toucher's place.

drills.name: Ask Lightly
steps: Choose two or three moments this week when you would normally touch someone without thinking, such as a greeting or comfort.
Instead, offer the touch in a way that can be declined, such as an open hand or a light question.
Notice how the other person responds, and whether they complete the gesture.
Note how asking felt to you.
Write down one way of asking that felt natural enough to keep.

drills.name: Power Check
steps: List the people over whom you hold some authority, such as staff, pupils, players or younger relatives.
For each, note whether you touch them, how, and whether they touch you in return.
Mark any touch that runs only one way.
For each marked touch, consider whether the person could easily refuse it.
Decide which touches you will replace with words or with gestures they can choose to complete.

quiz.q: A colleague did not pull away when you put your arm round her shoulders at a party. What does that tell you?
options: That she welcomed it, since she would have moved away if she had not
That she is interested in you and would welcome more closeness later
Very little: stillness may be freezing or politeness, not consent
That the touch was appropriate for that setting and that relationship
quiz.explain: People often go still when touched unexpectedly or unwantedly, especially at work or by someone with power. Stillness is not consent. Only a clear welcome or a clear yes tells you a touch was wanted.

quiz.q: What did Suvilehto and colleagues' body maps of permitted touch show across five countries?
options: The closer the bond, the more of the body that person was allowed to touch
People allowed strangers and partners to touch them in almost the same places
Each country produced a completely different map with no shared pattern at all
People allowed touch only on the hands, whatever the relationship involved
quiz.explain: Partners could touch almost anywhere, close family and friends the upper body, acquaintances mostly the arms and hands, strangers the hands alone. The pattern was shared across countries, with differences in how much touch each allowed.

quiz.q: What did Löken and colleagues find about C-tactile nerve fibres in the skin?
options: They respond most strongly to sharp, sudden pain anywhere on the body
They respond only to changes in temperature, not to any kind of pressure
They are found only in the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet
They respond best to slow, gentle stroking, which people find pleasant
quiz.explain: These fibres fired most at caress-like speeds, and their activity tracked how pleasant the touch felt. Skin seems built to register care, which makes unwanted touch as direct as welcome touch.

quiz.q: Your young nephew stiffens and turns away when relatives insist on a goodbye hug. What fits this chapter?
options: Insist on the hug, since it is rude to refuse relatives who love him
Let him choose another goodbye, such as a wave or a high five
Ignore it, since children always dislike hugs at that age anyway
Explain to him afterwards why relatives' feelings must come first
quiz.explain: His body is telling you what he does not want, and making him comply teaches him that his signals do not count. Offering a goodbye he can choose respects him and still lets him say goodbye.

quiz.q: In Hertenstein and colleagues' study, what could strangers communicate by touching only each other's forearm?
options: Nothing beyond whether the toucher was being friendly or unfriendly
Only pleasure and pain, and none of the more specific feelings tested
Several distinct feelings, such as gratitude, sympathy and anger
Only feelings that had first been agreed between them in advance
quiz.explain: Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy from touch alone, well above chance. Touch carries specific meaning, which is why its effects are so direct.

quiz.q: A friend's partner rests a hand on your arm for a long moment while talking with you at a party. What fits this chapter?
options: Note it in context and relationship, and do not take it as an invitation
Take it as a sign of attraction, and return the touch to show you noticed
Mention it quietly to your friend afterwards, in case it meant something
Move away sharply so that nobody could misunderstand what had happened
quiz.explain: A touch means what the relationship and setting make it mean, and many people touch the arm when talking. It does not grant permission for anything. If you are uncomfortable, a gentle step back is enough.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific touch you gave or received in the past year that was misread, by you or by the other person. Describe it: who, where on the body, the setting, and what was intended. What kind of touch did each of you take it to be? How did the person touched respond in the moments afterwards, and did anyone notice? What would you do differently now, and how would you ask?
reflection.guidance: Many people find their example at a party, a farewell or a moment of comfort, where kinds of touch blur. Try to separate what was intended from what was received, and notice whether the response was read at the time. The last question matters most. Find a way of asking that sounds like you, light enough to use without making a moment awkward.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read stillness as permission, mistaking a person's freezing or politeness for welcome. The second is the category error: offering a friendly or intimate touch where only a polite one was invited. The third is to use touch where you hold power, so that the person touched cannot easily refuse, and then to read their compliance as warmth. The fourth is to use touch as a technique to influence people, which this book refuses to teach. And the deepest failure is to apply to touch the method that works for every other channel, reading first and acting on the reading. With touch, reading is never enough. Ask lightly, accept any answer, and let the other person lead.
